utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the appearances of the parties, please. There's a part of the Prosecution that is hidden behind the pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Ekkehard Withopf, with Kimberly Fleming as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, which is rather far removed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic today, Edina Residovic, Defence Stephane Bourgon, and Alexis Demirdjian, attorney from Montreal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber bids good morning to all the parties: The Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. Today we have a new witness. But before calling the new witness, I would like to ask the Defence whether they filed their remarks, as I asked them to do, with regard to the motion of the Prosecution. I'm told that they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But we didn't manage to do it by 5.00, but we did by 7.00. We had some technical difficulties. It has been filed, both in electronic and paper form. It has been filed with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber notes that the Defence has been working all night in order to produce this document on time. Regarding the Prosecution, how many witnesses are planned for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's one witness on the schedule for today. In the event this witness can be finished prior to 1.45, there is a likelihood that we can call the second witness immediately after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Can I ask the usher to be kind enough to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. Are you hearing the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be kind enough to give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivanka Tavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of November, 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Maljine, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am currently unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm living in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you're going to testify now, is this the first time you're testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the text of a solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you will have to answer questions which the Prosecution, which is on your right, are going to put to you. And at the end of that examination, the Defence, which is on your left, with the attorney seated on your left, will have questions for you. The Judges, who are in front of you, may also have questions for you. And at the end of the questions of the Defence, the Prosecution may re-examine you. I am, therefore, going to give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Tavic.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, you told the Trial Chamber that you were born in Maljine. Where did you live in 1992 and in the first month of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At this point in time, 1992, and within the first month of 1993, members of which ethnicities were living in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Muslim ethnicity and members of the Croatian ethnicity were living in Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which group was in the majority.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: There were more Muslims, but not significantly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea in respect to the number of households for the Muslim group and for the Croat group?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Well, there may have been some 100 Croat households and between 150 and 200 Muslim households, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were the Croats and the Muslims living in the same area of Maljine, or were they living in separate areas?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Well, though it is one village by name, the ethnicities were separated. The part known as Gornje Maljine, which means "upper Maljine," inhabited by Croats; and the Donje Maljine, or "lower Maljine" were inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In 1992 and early 1993, what has been the relationship between the Croats and Serbs in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of 1993, there really were no problems between us, especially not on an ethnic basis. We had one school in the village. We went to school together. We socialised together. There were no incidents until the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time at which this good relationship changed?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: The first visible signs of change in the behaviour of the Muslims in our village appeared when the first Mujahedins appeared on the territory of Travnik municipality. It was then that in our village we started to notice Muslims, people we knew from before, but they changed in the way they dressed. They had beards grown and some Arab characteristics, which were quite unknown to us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These individuals which you are referring to as Mujahedin, when did you for the first time notice them in your geographical area?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I personally started coming across them at the end of 1992 in the town of Travnik. I would go to town often, so that -- they could be seen in the streets. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These Mujahedin, did they wear -- did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which sort of weapons.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly firearms, rifles. I don't know what make or type, but they were rifles, long barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Mujahedin, did they wear any military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had military uniforms, but individuals could be seen wearing different clothing. I really don't know how you call them. They were wearing some kind of clothing that was quite unusual, something we hadn't seen in our area before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, can you give the Trial Chamber a rough idea about the numbers of Mujahedin or how often have you seen them?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I went to town, I could see them. They became a daily occurrence. The largest groups could be seen in one of their charitable societies that they opened across the road from the police in Travnik. That is where they would gather in groups. You could always see them, 10 to 15 of them together, it depended. But you could see them every day in the streets. They became part of our daily lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Since the Mujahedin were armed, did you get any information or do you have any own knowledge where the Mujahedin were based?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Personally, on one occasion, as I was going into town by bus, I heard from a Muslim from our village that the Mujahedin had arrived at Mehurici, that there were quite a number of them there, how they would help them, that there were some in Poljanice. So that is how we learnt that they had come close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, was there a point in time when Maljine was attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you still recall as to when Maljine was attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the date.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: The actual attack occurred on the 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On the 7th of June, 1993, what did you do at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: The attack first started Postinje, early in the morning. It's a small village close to Maljine. I was actually awaked by the shooting that wasn't actually in my village, but nearby. And a couple of hours later, people from that part of the village brought in a man who was wounded in the leg and who was transported to the outpatients clinic. And during the transportation of this wounded man, the Muslims from Donje Maljine opened fire on the vehicle. And that is how the shooting actually started in my village. After the vehicle had taken the wounded man, my uncle was hit, Anto Talic, and then I, too, ran away from the house to the part where he had been wounded, and together with another three men, we brought him to the village. But as the shooting had escalated, there was no possibility of transporting him by car to the clinic, so that he was carried on foot across the hill, but he didn't survive. Unfortunately, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, you are mentioning a clinic. What was your function at the time on the 7th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: After this wounding happened and after the man died on the way up there, there was a doctor in the village and we realised that we had no choice but to organise ourselves in the village. And in a part of the village, in a large basement, we decided to form a sort of dispensary. And then I and two or three girls went round the village collecting sheets and medicines and bandages, and that is how we formed this dispensary in a basement. In view of the fact that night was falling, in the afternoon, as we were equipping the dispensary, already that afternoon there were some new wounded men; an older man, Anto Juric, had been hit in front of his house. His wife, who was running towards him, was also hit in the leg and she stayed lying on the road. He came to the dispensary. We managed to treat him. But when we tried to reach his wife, Mara, it was impossible, which was because the area was exposed and there was constant shooting, and she was left there until 9.00 in the evening. When night fell, then her sons went to pull her out. So that night, the night of the 7th, I spent in the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To which army did the attacking soldiers belong to?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: During the attack, did the attacking soldiers shout anything?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of June, early in the morning at dawn, about 3.30 or 4.00, when the main attack on Maljine started, when they had already entered the village and surrounded it from all sides, we heard some unusual calls of "Allah-U-Ekber," "Tekbir," the meaning of which I didn't know at all. I didn't know what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying that the attacking soldiers were from the ABiH, the Muslim army. Did you see any identifying features, any shoulder patches or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them in those days were wearing blue patches with lilies, which were the insignia of the BH army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Tavic, do you see a photo board in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please identify on this photo board the shoulder patch you were referring to a few seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: It is number 12, patch number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has identified on the Prosecution Exhibit P4 the patch numbered 12 as the one which was worn by the attacking ABiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, you were telling the Trial Chamber that the attacking soldiers were shouting "Tekbir," "Allah-U-Ekber," and other words you couldn't understand. Did they have any other things with them in a language you couldn't understand or couldn't read?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. If you're referring to the soldiers of the BH army that we saw just then, those were the only things they said I couldn't understand. But when the Mujahedin entered the village, there were many things that could not be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The attacking soldiers, did they have a flag with them?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what this flag was about.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: It was a big black flag. And somewhere in the middle something was written in Arabic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, do you know which unit of the ABiH attacked Maljine? Have you seen any identifying insignia?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has already answered that she only saw the insignia of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness, in answer to a previous question, clearly answered that she only saw the insignia of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which she identified as being the patch number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question of the Prosecution was whether the witness, in addition to the patch that she identified on P4, whether she saw any other patches or insignia. Madam Witness, when you were there - and you told us a moment ago that you were present during the attack - to the best of your memory, do you remember in addition to the patch that you identified any other distinctive patch? Did you notice any other? As it was more than ten years ago, do you remember it today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, things like that one does not forget. When the soldiers entered our village, we saw them face Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to face. And I had occasion to go to another part of the village with two of those soldiers to gather the civilians and the other wounded in other houses. One of the two soldiers who were escorting me had the insignia of the 314th Brigade. In front of a house where there were many civilians and a wounded pregnant woman, there were a number of soldiers of the BH army which bore the insignia of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you saw two types of insignia, of the 314th Brigade and of the 306th Brigade; is that right? And you're sure of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there a time on the 8th of June, 1993 when the fighting stopped?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the men from our village withdrew from the line that they had been manning, there were much fewer of them than the Muslim soldiers who were attacking them. We realised that we were totally encircled. And then the women who were hiding in shelters talked us into surrendering, because there was no other way out. Then we spoke to the soldiers who were in that part of the village, and then the doctor made a big flag from the smaller Red Cross flags. She left the house. She waved the flag and in that way showed the army that we were surrendering. And then somebody on the other side shouted, "Stop shooting. They are surrendering." A few minutes later the shooting stopped indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After the surrender of the Croats, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: When we surrendered, the doctor went to a group of Muslim soldiers with that flag. After a certain time, she returned and she said that they wanted us to gather all the weapons and bring them to them. However, the men who carried weapons were afraid for their safety. They said that there was nobody to guarantee their safety. Then the doctor went back to talk to the soldiers, and the message she brought back was that there was no other way out; either we were to surrender or they would continue shooting. And then the men decided to surrender their weapons. The doctor collected the weapons, together with a girl, and they brought the weapons to the Muslim soldiers on the other side. Then the Muslim soldiers entered the dispensary, in that part of the village, and they separated soldiers on one side, separated soldiers on one side, men on another side, women and children on a third side. They told us to remain in the dispensary with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Amongst the soldiers, the defending soldiers of Maljine, was there any of your family members?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a brother. It is a small village, and everybody -- mostly everybody is connected with family ties in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber the name of your brother.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: My brother was an able-bodied man, and he was on the line of the defence. His name was Miroslav. However, the other brother had been wounded. He was not able-bodied. He was among the wounded. His name was Stipo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to your brother Stipo Tavic and the other soldiers which had been -- which had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Once we surrendered, all the civilians and soldiers were lined in a column -- I apologise. And that column was escorted by Muslim soldiers and set off for Mehurici. Since the wounded could not move, we asked for a truck to be provided for them. Once the truck was found, we put the wounded on that truck. My brother was among them. However, although we were supposed to go with the wounded and their escorts, there was an argument among the Muslims, so the Mujahedins who had entered the village and the BH army soldiers, they simply jumped on the truck and took it away in an unknown direction. Thank you. Later on I learnt that that truck ended up on the road towards Bikose. The wounded were taken off that truck, and together with other men, they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, if you need a break, the Trial Chamber is certainly very well prepared to have a short break.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If you can give me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to make a five-minute break. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, can you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, madam. The Chamber would like to tell you that whenever you want to interrupt the testimony, you should tell us. Whenever you feel that you are not up to answering questions, we will accommodate your wish for a break. Can we now continue? The Prosecution, you may resume your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Tavic, you were telling the Trial Chamber that a number of Croats, amongst them your brother, were put on a truck by the Mujahedin. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who else in addition to your brother was put on this truck?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, the Prosecutor says that the witness stated that some of the Croats, amongst whom her brother, were put on a truck by the Mujahedin. As far as I can see in the transcript, this was not said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please rephrase your question, because effectively the Defence has the right in objecting that this is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, do you still recall who put your brother, Stipo Tavic, on the truck?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: It was us who put the wounded on the truck, but the truck was driven away by the Mujahedin, and that's the source of the misunderstanding. Besides my brother, we put other wounded on the truck; those were the wounded who were in the infirmary. I can give you their names. All of them were executed except for Mara Juric, who was taken off the truck before the truck stopped, and she was left on the road. In addition to my brother, there was also Luka Balta, Jozo Balta, Predrag Puselja, Anto Matic, Mara Juric, and Srecko Bobas. They were all seriously wounded and they were all bedridden. They couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to the rest of the Croat civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: The rest of the civilians and soldiers were taken in a group towards Mehurici village. However, when they arrived at Poljanice they were intercepted by the Mujahedin and they separated the soldiers wearing uniforms from other -- and other able-bodied men, according to their estimate. However, there was a 16-year-old boy, Stjepan Volic. And they were all taken back towards Bikose. And together with the wounded, these people were also shot dead. However, luckily enough, a few of them managed to escape, so we learnt what had happened at Bikose. When the Mujahedin took the wounded away, I remained with the doctor and the other woman who was in the dispensary. A person called Ibrahim came. He was from Kotor Varos. He told us that he would transfer us personally to Mehurici. At that moment, another soldier came up to us and said that the car that had taken the wounded pregnant woman broke down, so we took another girl who was wounded in the leg. Ibrahim found another car, and he personally took us to Mehurici village. When we arrived in that village, we stopped in front of the surgery in Mehurici. There was a lot of people there. Everybody was shouting at us, cursing us. I can't remember the exact words. However, the soldiers did escort us all the way to the surgery. Dr. Ribo was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there, a remarkable man he was. At one moment, people were pushing to get in to take us out. He stood up against them and told them, "Only over my dead body will you be able to take these people out of here." He really helped us. We were with him in the surgery. He helped us to take care of the pregnant woman's wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, may I stop you here. You were mentioning a surgeon, Ibrahim, who took you to Mehurici. This Ibrahim, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself to us as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was he a commander of the ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He bore the insignia of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to leaving Maljine, did you notice what the ABiH soldiers did in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: As they were passing through -- as I was passing through the village, I could see in front of the houses that the soldiers were getting into the house and out of them. In front of my house, there was a lot of soldiers already. They entered houses. And the car that was in the garage was already standing in front of the house. As we continued walking through the village, in front of Mirko Kramar's house three men were standing. One of them was Semir Prcanovic. The doctor asked Ibrahim to stop. She got out of the car, and she told them, "Shame on you. You have already started plundering, and we are still in the village." The only thing that I took with me from the house were my keys. When I returned to my house in 1996, I didn't even find the door for that key. The only thing that I'm sorry that I lost are my photos, my memories. This is as if we have never lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to Mehurici, what happened to you and your group in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: As we sent the wounded pregnant woman from the dispensary, some soldiers came to fetch us with a car. They transferred us to some sort of a command. They brought us into a building which was the Mehurici school. They took us into a room. We found a soldier there. I remember that he had all the ranks, but I can't remember what his rank was. But he was a regular soldier, and his composure was very professional. He introduced himself to us as Sanjin from Kotor Varos. And he told us that this was enough for us to know. He told us that he would ask a few questions. However, he asked us some very general questions. Then another person entered the room. His last name was Fazlic. He was very rude. He was very impertinent. He shouted, cursed, made a lot of noise. But we did not have anything to say in addition to what we knew that had happened in our village. He saw that this would take him nowhere, so a few hours later they released us. We wanted to see what had happened to the other fellow villagers, and they took us to the gymnasium. In that school, when we arrived there, we saw that there was a state of chaos. The people were frightened. They were asking after various people. They didn't know what had happened to the people who had been separated. And they told us that all the men had been separated from the group and taken away, that they had been intercepted by the Mujahedin. Smajo Tarakcija was at the entrance to the gymnasium. He took our names as the representative of the civilian protection. When I entered the gymnasium, two Mujahedin came up to me. They started tearing the Red Cross band from me. They were talking to the doctor and they asked her if she spoke English. They pointed to my neck, and my uncle was also there. I managed to tear away from them. In any case, there was a state of chaos in that big hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were telling the Trial Chamber that soldiers brought you to a building which you identified as the Mehurici Elementary School. Soldiers of which army brought you to this building?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Those were BH army soldiers. There were no Mujahedin at that point. We saw them only when we got into this gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, I'm now going to show you a photograph. The photograph will appear in front -- on the screen in front of you. And we also have the respective hard copies available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of the Chamber and the Defence, this photograph was taken in the course of the investigation against the accused in the year 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: This is the primary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the school you are referring to -- you were referring to as the building you were brought to by ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does the sports hall you were referring to a few minutes ago, does it form part of this building or this complex of buildings?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, can you give us the number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before that, can she put her initials and the date on this exhibit. Madam Witness, can you put your initials and the date, today's date, on the photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show it to the Defence. Madam Registrar, what is the number then? Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P28. Before I give you the floor, Prosecution, the Judge of the Chamber has another question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam witness, I have two questions for you. The first is the following: When the soldiers of the BH army attacked your village, were there any HVO soldiers in your village? That is my first question. My second question: Was your brother a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my village, there were members of the HVO. There were some 20 of them, and they were all locals. My brother was a member of the HVO, but ever since February, when he was wounded, he was no longer active, because he had -- his legs were fixed and immobile and he could only move with the help of crutches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Witness, that means that on that day your brother was not dressed in military uniform; he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in civilian. He was wearing a sweatsuit. This can be proven. And later on, when his remains were found, he was wearing this same sweatsuit or jogging suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask -- and you told me that he had crutches, because he had been wounded earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he got onto the truck, he had those crutches with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, I'm now going to show you another photograph. The photograph will appear on the screen in front of you, and we also have the hard copies available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of the Trial Chamber and for the information of the Defence, this photograph was taken in 2002 in the course of the investigation against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, you were refer -- sorry, you were referring to, a few minutes ago, to a sports hall you were brought to. What can you see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: That is the sports hall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, can you identify this sports hall as the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is that sports hall in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please sign this photograph and date it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the Prosecution wishes to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you give me an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The sports hall in the Mehurici Elementary School you just identified, Ms. Tavic, how many people were there when you joined them?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: There was about 350 of us, and there were also civilians from another village who had sought shelter in our village. So in addition to civilians from Maljine, there were those from Postinje, Podovi, Orasac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people who were in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: We were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were these about 350 Croats detained at the sports hall -- in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken there by force. Though at the interrogation they tried to persuade us that they had sheltered us there for our own safety and that they would quickly take us back to our homes, as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you and the other detainees stay voluntarily in the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who guarded the sports hall of the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: For the first couple of days, there were no organised guards. In the corridor leading to the gym, there were many soldiers, Mujahedin, some sort of policemen. It was always crowded. However, our doctor talked to one of the commanders and requested that no one be allowed to enter the gym without her being notified, so that the people could calm down. There were a lot of children crying and screaming. You can imagine, 350 people were there. And after these requests of hers, they were met and then we had regular guards consisting of two members of the BH army and two policemen. They called them reservists. So that there were four men at the door all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, could you identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Witness, you have just told us, looking at the transcript, that there were officers. How could you tell that there were officers, since you were detained in the gym when these policemen were on the -- somewhere else? How did you know that they were there? Did you understand the meaning of my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean how we knew that they were in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the presence of officers who were in the corridor somewhere else. So I'm asking you: Did you see them or did someone else tell you that they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them, because there was a corridor from the hall and it was always full of these soldiers and policemen. And from that corridor, there was a toilet that we could use, which was next to the gym, so that there was a long queue. We all had to wait to go to the toilet. And as we were queueing up, we could see what was happening in the corridor and outside in the yard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a last point of clarification: What distinction are you making between an officer and a simple soldier? How do you make the distinction between an officer and a simple soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question. I said, to make myself quite clear, that in the corridor there were always many soldiers, Mujahedin, and policemen. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not -- that doesn't quite correspond. Because a moment ago you said that there were officers, and now you're telling us that there were Mujahedin and policemen but not officers. These were policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say "officers." I said that our doctor wanted to talk to one of their commanders in order to have normal guards there, instead of so many soldiers being there. And then, after that, she spoke to one of their commanders in the corridor. One of the soldiers took her to their command. She spoke to them, and they promised to provide guards. And after that, we had normal guards at the door, four men. Up until then, the corridor was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, you were telling the Trial Chamber that you have been guarded or that in the corridors there were Mujahedin. Were there also any other ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many soldiers in uniform. And after the guards became regular guards consisting of two soldiers and two policemen, the soldiers were from the 306th Brigade. They were regulars, neat, and I think they changed shifts every four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How did you get to know that these soldiers were from the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I already said they wore the insignia of the brigade. These guards who were guarding us, from that day up until the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were telling the Trial Chamber that there have been about 350 detainees. And you also mentioned that there were babies amongst them. Can you please, in rough numbers, detail how many men, how many women, and how many children.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly, 80 per cent were women and children. The rest were men, mostly elderly. Babies, I think we had about 25. I think the youngest was under one month old and she was crying most of the time. She had to be carried around, because she was a very tiny infant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the food you received during your detention.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: For the first two or three days they would bring into the hall a table and put on it pieces of bread made from flour that was used as cattle feed and some cheese, pieces of cheese. And people could take as much as they wanted. It was very disorderly and very poor quality. After that, we asked that we distribute the food, to put some order in it. And then we received two meals a day; one in the morning, one in the afternoon. In the morning they would again bring in a piece of bread made of this same kind of flour and quite a large can or -- tin that would be shared by six. And in the afternoon again, we would get a small piece of bread and some boiled rice, a spoonful, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the hygienic conditions in the Mehurici Elementary School sports hall.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine. 350 of us to one toilet and which would get blocked up every five minutes or so. We had to keep cleaning it. And a quarrel could get started over it because one had to queue up to get to the toilet. We would get clean water towards the end, and we had to ask for it because there were so many small babies that we had to bathe. And we had a wounded man, and he needed to be -- his wounds needed to be dressed. So in the middle of that period, we would get about 5 litres of warm water to be able to bathe the babies and to treat the wounds of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were telling us that amongst the 350 detainees there were a number of men. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how the men were treated.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not well. They were taken out to work during the day. I don't know. They went to dig pits, to clean the sewage. At least, that's what they told us when they came back. They always came back dirty. Some of the men were taken out for interrogation. Some of them, when they came back, had visible traces of mistreatment, but they kept quiet about it because if they were to say anything, they would fare even worse. So no one dared say anything. People just kept quiet and suffered in silence. I remember Zeljo Puselj. He had been wounded in the hand, in the arm. And he was bleeding a lot. He had a serious wound. The doctor wanted him to be treated immediately and taken to Zenica, but they wouldn't allow that. They apparently needed him for some information, and he was taken out frequently and each time he came back in worse condition. And afterwards, when we were exchanged, he was transferred to the hospital in Zenica. And he's an invalid to this day as a consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, for how long have you been detained in the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: From the 6th to the 24th of June, 1993. Sorry, from the 8th until the 24th. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long have the other detainees been detained in the Mehurici Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: When we were about to be exchanged, the day prior to that they separated the men and took them somewhere else and said that they would be exchanged in another exchange procedure. But as far as I can recollect - but I cannot claim that with any certainty - but I think it was only a year later that they were exchanged, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know how and who negotiated for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Before we were exchanged, Mr. Salko Beba arrived with a group of men. He introduced himself as a man who was in charge of exchanges, and he told us to be ready, that we would probably be exchanged in the course of the next day. I remember that the exchange was to be in the morning, and then the expectation went on until the afternoon. About 3.00 the bus us arrived. We got onto them. And we were driven then towards Dolac. Throughout that time, I remember we were seen off at Mehurici by the local population with all kinds of shouts and curses. As we were passing through Donje Maljine, I saw my village, which had already been destroyed, abandoned. What hadn't been destroyed had been moved into. And then I realised that we would never go back there again. The exchange took place at Dolac. After that, some went to Bila, some to Vitez, some to Busovaca. People did the best they could. They found accommodation with relatives or friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Salko Beba, the person you described of having been in charge of exchanges, was he an ABiH soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know this gentleman from before, since his sister went to secondary school with me. So I met him even before. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did he have a rank, a military rank at this point in time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember that, because in those days I wasn't interested in the military, nor was I familiar with ranks. So I am unable to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Tavic, thank you very much. For the time being, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before the break, I would like to ask the witness to tell me, if she can: She told us that there were 350 of them in this gym. There were elderly people. There were women. There were children and babies, in fact, and that she stayed there from the 8th to the 24th, that is, 16 days. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning when you were detained, were you told why they were holding you and the babies? Did you know why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we didn't. I mentioned earlier on that when the three of us were being interrogated, then this Fazlic told us that we should consider ourselves lucky, because they had brought us there to save us from our own people and that we had nothing to worry about and that we could go back to our homes the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now going to have a break of 25 minutes. And after the break, it will be the turn of the Defence to question you as part of the cross-examination, as the Prosecution has told us they have no more questions for you. So you will be able to rest for 25 minutes, and we will be resuming the hearing in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming our session. If I understood you well, the Prosecution does not have any more questions; therefore, I'm giving the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'm Edina Residovic, and I'm defending General Hadzihasanovic. I'm going to ask you a few questions about the things that you have already spoken about earlier this morning. First of all, Ms. Tavic, is it correct that you already had an interview with the representatives of the OTP and that in 2000 you gave a statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated in Sarajevo on the eve of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us this morning - and can you please confirm it - when the war started, you were in Maljine. After graduation, you did not leave your village.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that Maljine village was divided into two separate villages, Gornje Maljine, with a Croat population; and Donje Maljine, with a Bosniak population. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that above your village there is Mount Vlasic, on which there were defence lines facing the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that when the troops that were manning the lines up there, both the BH army troops and the HVO army troops, would go to their positions from the surrounding villages and that they would have to pass in the vicinity of your village? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Only our village lads would go through our village. There was another road for others, so Muslims from Donje Maljine and boys from our village -- the Croats from our village could go through our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the soldiers from Gornje and Donje Maljine would go through your village to go to the lines?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To my learned friend's question, you answered that at the end of 1992 and particularly at the beginning of 1993, when you went to visit your brother in the Travnik hospital, in Travnik you saw quite a number of foreigners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me if I say that these foreigners differed from the local population, both the Bosniak and the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They looked Arab to you. Some of them -- or most of them had turbans on their heads or some other head covers and they spoke a language that we do not understand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated - and can you please confirm it - that you saw them in groups gathering around the Muslim charitable society which was across the road from the civilian police station?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the Merhamet humanitarian society, or was there a humanitarian society that was founded by the foreigners?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of the name. I know that it was a Muslim humanitarian society. But who the founder of that society was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on one occasion in their presence you recognised a schoolmate of yours who later on finished religious school and became a hodza?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that to the Prosecutor in the year 2000, although later on a friend tried to convince me that the opposite was true. So I'm now in two minds. I don't know whether this was this gentleman or not. A friend of mine, who was more familiar with the situation in Travnik, told me that it was somebody else who looked very much like that schoolmate of mine, so I wouldn't be able to confirm that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Travnik, on several occasions you noticed a number of refugees who had arrived from Jajce, Kotor Varos, and the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I myself collected humanitarian aid in my village, and on every Thursday we would take that to the secondary school in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to the events that you testified about that unfortunately happened on the 7th and the 8th of June in your village. To the Prosecutor's question, you said that on that morning you were in the makeshift dispensary that was organised by Dr. Ljuba Puselja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the HVO lines had already fallen, some other people arrived in your dispensary. They were civilians from your village. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, at one moment, about 20 HVO soldiers who were withdrawing from the line also arrived in your dispensary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, as you described to us earlier this morning, because of the fact that there were wounded and children there, Dr. Ljuba Puselja decided to hoist an improvised Red Cross flag in order to start negotiating with the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that one of the ABiH soldiers, as soon as he saw the flag, issued an order for the fire to stop.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A few moments later, somebody from the group shouted, "Stop. Hold the fire. Stop firing."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were with Dr. Ljuba Puselja at the moment when the BH army soldier introduced himself to you as Ibrahim from Kotor Varos, and you thought that he was their commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He told you'll that they were the ABiH army and that nothing bad would happen to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your request, he enabled you to look at all the houses in the village in order to find other villagers who had not managed to arrive safely at the dispensary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This all lasted a certain time.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long it lasted. I remember that it rained heavily, the roads were slippery. I was escorted by two soldiers, and we went from one house to another shouting, "Is there anybody there? Come out." So I wouldn't be able to tell you whether this lasted a half an hour or an hour or even longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed that this soldier, Ibrahim, had already been a bit edgy and he rushed you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, he told you that he wanted you to hurry up because he was afraid that Mujahedins would arrive and that he would not be able to guarantee your safety.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mujahedins at that time were on Greda. That was the former defence line. They were shouting from up there. But it was impossible to rush so many people. How could you rush the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you could notice on Ibrahim that he was also restless and that he was also afraid that the Mujahedin might arrive.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. If I know somebody, then I know I can trust them. If I don't know them, then how can I trust them? But I believed that they could protect us the way civilians deserved to be protected. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor's question, you answered that Dr. Ljuba Puselja asked Ibrahim to give her a truck to transport the wounded and Ibrahim granted that request; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you took a truck from Franjo Pranjes and you put the wounded on that truck yourself.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the truck, together with a soldier, whereas others were helping us pull the wounded onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Puselja also asked Ibrahim to allow you to accompany the wounded on the truck and he accepted that.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim also granted your request for the pregnant woman not to be driven on a truck but by a vehicle, because the doctor said that the truck would not be a suitable means of transportation for her.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. She was in an advanced stage of pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after all these preparations, at one point a group of five men arrived in the village? Among them you recognised three as being foreign. You thought that one of them was an interpreter and one of them was a local Mujahedin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They all sported beards.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all had beards. They wore different clothes. They were very rude. They were shouting. And they were different and they behaved differently than anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim entered into an argument with them. They didn't allow them to approach. However, they jumped onto the truck and they set the truck in motion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they arrived, I was on the truck. I was putting the wounded on the truck. And then I heard an argument. One of the wounded told me, "Ivanka, turn around. They're shouting. They're calling your name." One of them asked me to get off the truck and I saw one of those Mujahedins pulling the doctor by her arm and showing signs that he would kill her. Ibrahim pulled her aside. They started quarreling, and at one point they just took the truck and took it away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, a couple of questions about your arrival in Mehurici. You said that together with the pregnant woman you arrived in front of the surgery in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was an -- the ABiH surgery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that I -- that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Dr. Ribo and Dr. Puselja started administering help to this injured woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He prevented the mob from insulting you or hurting you.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were pushing through the door; however, he stopped them by saying, "You can have them only over my dead body," and I'm ever so grateful to him for having done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ribo was an ABiH army doctor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after having examined the pregnant woman, he secured her transportation to the hospital in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, when the three wounded -- the three persons who had escaped from the execution site in Bikose were brought to Mehurici, among them there was one person with serious injuries. Dr. Ribo took came of him and sent him to the hospital in Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Darko Puselja, he had fainted. And I know that Dr. Puselja insisted on him being treated and transferred to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were at all times helping Dr. Puselja, you are aware of the fact that all this time Dr. Ribo provided the doctor with all the necessary drugs and medical equipment, all that he had at his disposal in his surgery.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would arrive and offer his help. However, whatever medicines he offered, our doctor already had. So we did not need all these medicines, because she already had all the bare necessities that were needed for such situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the primary school, you were also visited by a member of the civilian protection from Mehurici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: I remember a member of the civilian protection from Donje Maljine. He took our names on the first day. That's the only person I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that later on, when order was restored, you were guarded by the civilian reserve police and you were aware of that fact because they had the insignia of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that they told us that that's -- that was their name "Reserve Police."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to express to you my condolences about the loss that you suffered during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence of Mr. Kubura, do you wish to ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Kubura does not have any questions to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would like to ask a few questions myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in your village and you helped the doctor, we could understand from your testimony that there was shooting, that there was gunfire. The members of the HVO, did they also open fire during that stage after some of them had been injured?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: During the morning hours of the 7th of June, there was no gunfire in the village. There was gunfire in the neighbouring village of Postinje. And only when one of their wounded passed through our village in a car to Guca Gora, then fire was opened from Donje Maljine on that car that was passing through the village. At that moment, fire was returned from our lines. Until then, we did not have any incidents. There were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So you can confirm to us that fire was returned from your lines. And according to your knowledge, did the enemy army, the opposition army, were they wounded? Were there any casualties? You were in some sort of a dispensary in a medical institution. Did they bring any other wounded to your institution from the other side?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. While I was in Mehurici, we were visited by Fadil Prcanovic. He was the president of the civilian protection. And he said that luckily enough they didn't have any casualties and that all the bodies that were killed on our side would be buried in our cemetery according to our customs. However, this didn't come true. We still don't know where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Owing to a question put to you by the Prosecution, we learnt that you graduated from a university. What did you graduate in?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA TAVIC
utterances.text: It was tourism and the catering industry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Prosecution, do you have any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your testimony is now over, as the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges have asked you questions. We understand that this was especially painful for you, because the questions related to facts that affected you personally. So the Chamber and the Judges of this Chamber wish to convey their condolences, as did the Defence, for the loss of your loved ones who were victims of this conflict. Thank you for your testimony, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the next witness will be available at 11.45. But before that, I should like to address two points: The first is that we have been informed this morning of a motion of the Defence regarding a motion filed by the Prosecution regarding the list of witnesses and the exhibits. As you know, we ordered that the Defence should brief us on their position before the 12th of January. The Defence has informed us of a series of difficulties in connection with these documents, and they indicate in particular that they still have not received from the Prosecution all the exhibits. Therefore, it would be desirable for the Prosecution to contact the Defence to address outstanding problems. And if certain problems have not been resolved that are covered by the documents of this morning, that the Prosecution address to us a response to this document in writing so that we are able to make a determination by the 12th of January. A second point I should like to address has to do with the procedure of producing documents which are marked for identification. I have noted that those documents are first shown to the witness, and all of us have a copy: The Defence, the Judges, a copy for the Registry, and a copy for our legal officer. It appears to me to be useful for the accused that before these documents are distributed that the accused are shown those documents, for them to make their observations in writing, and then that they be given to the Defence. So should the accused -- if the accused say nothing, it is very difficult for them to make any observations themselves to the counsel except by writing bits of paper. So it would be better for them to have this document in their hands and then to give them to their Defence immediately. If no one has any objection, in the future, when the Prosecution wishes to produce a document, the Registry will give the copies to everyone, and the accused will also have copies in front of them. They will write down any observations they may have and pass them on to the Defence. Does the Defence agree with this procedure, which can only be beneficial for the accused? I should like to hear the oral response of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we believe that that would be extremely useful, because you yourself see that our clients often send us bits of paper to remind us of certain facts which are of importance for their defence. And we feel that this would be very significant for the documents that are being produced for the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we fully subscribe to your advice and your opinion and feel that this would be very useful for our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has no objections against such a procedure. In respect to the first issue, allegedly missing documents, this appears to be more of a problem of a technical nature, and the Prosecution is in contact with Defence counsel to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note that this suggestion of the Chamber is acceptable, and we will put it into practice and it will be beneficial for the Defence and the accused. Regarding documents, I dare to hope that the problems that have been raised will be settled, and I should like to Prosecution to let us know in writing as soon as possible what its position is with regard to the points indicated on pages 8 and 9, and all the requests made by the Defence to the Chamber concerning points A through to F. The Prosecution is telling me that the witness will be available in 15 minutes' time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you allow me, please, to confer with my colleague for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I address the Court with two issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the Prosecution confer amongst themselves first, and after that we will hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. I apologise. The witness was scheduled for tomorrow morning, and my colleague is still in the middle of the proofing session. We didn't anticipate, due to the fact that the cross-examination didn't take very long, that the witness would need to be called today. The witness, however, will be ready for examination-in-chief at 12.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me that it won't be at quarter to 12.00 but, rather, at half past 12.00? Because you first said he would be ready tomorrow, but now you're telling me 12.30, so it's still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's still today. 12.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And tomorrow you plan to continue with this witness and you have another witness? How many witnesses are we going to have tomorrow? Because tomorrow is the last day of the year for our hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We will continue with this witness tomorrow, and there is no other witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the witness whose testimony will begin at 12.30 will be our last witness for this week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's completely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel has two points to raise: Yes. The first point has to do with the next witness; namely, as the Prosecutor just said, we have received the list of witnesses for this week. Today only Ms. Tavic was planned for, and the next witness for tomorrow. Of course, it is better to finish our work early. But it is not so good that we weren't fully prepared for this witness today. However, we quite agree in having the examination-in-chief today. However, as the Defence doesn't know how long the examination-in-chief may last, I would like to request from the Trial Chamber even if the examination-in-chief is completed today, that we start the cross-examination tomorrow, because we haven't brought any of the documents relating to this witness with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this first point, there's no problem. Because if we start at half past 12.00, the examination-in-chief will take place today and the cross-examination tomorrow. And as we plan to finish at 13.45, we have to plan for that. So there's no problem regarding that. What is your second point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second point, Mr. President, is linked to a continuing and acute problem that the Defence is confronted with and which you too have been able to take note of during these three weeks of trial. That is the question of translation of documents. We have already at our own initiative had documents translated which we used in this Tribunal. Following your instructions, that a document which is not translated by simultaneously interpreted in the courtroom, we have seen that that doesn't function too well. The Prosecution would not accept this method of producing documents because he hadn't seen it in advance in a language he understands, which we appreciate. And we do feel it is difficult to accept a document in that way. And that is why we have had to only identify two or three documents, mark them for identification until they are translated; and secondly, we sought to avoid producing any document which we felt was not so relevant and which could be accepted without translation. Following suggestions of the Trial Chamber, we have submitted for urgent translation a part of the documents relating to Dusina. We still haven't received the translations of those documents and we have already heard about events in Guca Gora, in Brajkovici, in Miletici, and Maljine. Therefore, even the documents for the first event are not available to the Defence and the Trial Chamber in translation, not to mention others which we still haven't given for translation, because the service simply is not able to keep track in time. We would therefore request, Mr. President, that the Registry be asked to allow us additional hours for working translations of documents which we could use for the cross-examination. This would not entail a significant number of documents, and we feel that with some additional 30 hours per month for each Defence team we would be able to ensure translations for all the documents that would be used in the

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, I believe that this problem will escalate and we will find ourselves in a situation to which we cannot find a solution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this important problem has the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have nothing to add. This is a common position of both Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the opinion of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the last issue raised by my learned colleague, the Prosecution does appreciate that translations are necessary for the proceedings. This is an issue between the Registry and Defence counsel, and I'm sure the parties, meaning the Registry and Defence counsel, will find a solution. It would certainly be very beneficial for the conduct of this trial if such translations would be done in due time. In relation to the first issue, Your Honours, Mr. President, you already mentioned that there will be no cross-examination of the next witness today. I wish to add that it would be very good to know, very beneficial for the Prosecution to know in advance if the Defence could give us some sort of indication how long they intend to cross-examine the witness. That would certainly be very helpful for our planning and for our planning, in order not to waste the court time. In addition, I wish to inform the Trial Chamber - and this is a different issue - that the Prosecution disclosed on last Friday, the 12th of December, the B/C/S translation of the military expert report to the Defence, and it's the understanding of the Prosecution that Defence announced that within five days after the disclosure of the B/C/S translation they would file a motion in respect to the military expert report. To date -- the Prosecution notes that to date we haven't received such a motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before your ruling was made, we stated clearly that we would provide our response to that report five days after receiving the Bosnian version. It is true that on Friday, at 6.00 p.m. we received the Bosnian translation. However, Mr. President, your ruling was that we should make that response by the 12th. We shall certainly do so much earlier than that, than the deadline you have set. Thank you.
